Koopman-inspired predictors provide a structured representation of nonlinear dynamics by evolving observables through finite-dimensional linear maps. A fixed lifted transition, however, can be restrictive when the measured state does not determine the relevant operating condition. This paper develops a history-conditioned scheduled predictor in which a state-preserving temporal lifting map is complemented by a context-dependent low-rank transition and a measurement-dependent input modulation. The transition and input matrices are bounded functions of a history context and the current lifted measurement, respectively. For fixed scheduling signals the predictor is linear in the lifted state and input, while recursive scheduling remains generally nonlinear. We analyze this distinction directly. Under common-history, work-domain, Lipschitz, and one-step residual conditions, we derive a finite-horizon open-loop prediction bound. For control, a nominal rollout supplies scheduling matrices that are frozen over the horizon, yielding an LTV prediction model and a convex quadratic program under polyhedral input constraints. We further derive a finite-horizon bound between the complete scheduled model and its frozen approximation, and state a conditional cost-suboptimality result relative to the global optimum of the complete problem. The results are deliberately limited to finite-horizon open-loop prediction and conditional optimization error; they do not assert closed-loop stability, recursive feasibility, real-time performance, or hardware-control guarantees.

Learning a predictive model for a nonlinear controlled system is useful in a control setting when the model can be evaluated recursively and incorporated into a control calculation. Classical system identification provides a broad collection of state-space and input--output tools \cite{ljung1999system,vanoverschee1994n4sid,nelles2020nonlinear}. Koopman methods offer a complementary viewpoint: nonlinear state evolution is represented through linear evolution of observables, and finite-dimensional approximations can be used for prediction and control \cite{koopman1931hamiltonian,mezic2005spectral,williams2015data,korda2018linear,brunton2022modern}. The finite-dimensional approximation, however, depends on the selected coordinates and on how operating-condition variation is represented.

When an instantaneous measurement is not a sufficient description of the relevant dynamics, delay coordinates and recurrent representations can provide additional temporal information \cite{brunton2017chaos,kamb2020timedelay,arbabi2017ergodic,das2019delay,shenoy2025temporal,han2024robust}. A temporal lifting map can therefore encode a finite measurement history rather than a single sample. This addresses a representation problem but does not by itself solve a transition-model problem: all histories may still be propagated by one global lifted matrix. Context-dependent Koopman models and related temporal operator constructions instead allow the effective transition to vary with a recent trajectory or operating condition \cite{liu2023koopa,li2025mamko,forootani2025deepkoopformer}. The present work combines these two ideas while retaining a structured, bounded low-rank modulation around a shared nominal transition.

Recursive prediction creates a second difficulty. The history used to train a one-step map is formed from measured samples, whereas deployment recursively updates the history with predicted measurements. The resulting context can differ from the context seen during one-step training. Thus, a small one-step residual does not by itself provide a multi-step guarantee. The analysis below makes the shared initial history and the recursive window update explicit, and treats the resulting delay coupling rather than replacing it with an instantaneous error recurrence.

The same scheduling dependence creates a control trade-off. If the scheduling variables are recomputed from the decision-dependent predicted trajectory, the complete finite-horizon problem is generally nonlinear and nonconvex. Freezing the scheduling matrices along a nominal rollout produces an LTV approximation and a convex quadratic program for polyhedral input constraints. This is a modeling approximation, not an assertion that the complete scheduled problem is linear. The distinction is central to the control analysis.

This construction is related to gain scheduling and quasi-linear parameter-varying control, where a linear model is indexed by an operating condition or scheduling signal \cite{rugh2000gain,leith1998velocity,cisneros2016qlmpc,cisneros2020qlpv}. It also differs from real-time iteration methods, which perform a single sequential-quadratic-programming update for a nonlinear optimal-control problem \cite{diehl2005realtime,gros2020rti}. Here the frozen matrices are generated from a history-aware nominal rollout and the result is analyzed as a finite-horizon LTV approximation. The paper therefore does not transfer the stability, convergence, or timing guarantees that may hold for particular gain-scheduled or RTI schemes.

\item We formulate a state-preserving, history-conditioned scheduled predictor with a low-rank bounded modulation of a nominal transition and a separate measurement-dependent input modulation. The two scheduling variables are separated as a modeling choice; no parameter-identifiability claim is made.

Section~\ref{sec:experiments} records the experimental protocol while intentionally leaving numerical results for a later, separately verified stage. Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} summarizes the established scope and limitations.

The model and the control analysis use a common-history convention. All compared rollouts start from the same measured window and past-input window and from the same $\vz_0=g_\theta(\mX_k)$. For a predicted index $j<0$, a history slot reads the corresponding measured past sample rather than a fictitious negative-time latent state. After each step, the oldest measurement slot is replaced by $C_x\vz_{i+1}$ and the oldest input slot by $\vu_i$.

The intended architecture is a patch-based temporal Transformer encoder \cite{vaswani2017attention,nie2023time}. We impose the implementation constraint $p\mid P$: the history is partitioned into $P/p$ contiguous patches, each patch is linearly embedded, augmented with positional encoding, processed by a Transformer encoder, and pooled before projection to the hidden lifted coordinates. The current measurement is concatenated to this projection as in \eqref{eq:state_preserving_lifting}. Thus, the theoretical map $g_\theta$ abstracts the architecture while the state-preserving readout and the recursive propagation interface remain explicit. The context map $C_\phi$ is a separate feed-forward map of the flattened measurement and past-input windows. These architectural details specify the intended temporal map; the bounds below use only the stated Lipschitz and work-domain conditions.

The map $\mA$ is scheduled by history, while $\mB$ is scheduled by the current measured component of the lifted state. This separation is a parameterization choice: it does not assert that the physical input effect is independent of history and does not, by itself, establish parameter identifiability.

This paper formulated a history-conditioned scheduled predictor with a state-preserving temporal lifting, a bounded low-rank history-conditioned transition, and a measurement-dependent input modulation. The scheduled form preserves linear propagation when the scheduling signals are fixed, while its recursive use remains generally nonlinear. The finite-horizon prediction result makes the history-window coupling explicit and gives a conditional open-loop bound under common-history, work-domain, Lipschitz, and residual conditions.

The scope is intentionally limited. The results do not establish stability, recursive feasibility, real-time deadlines, exact optimality of an approximate numerical solver, or physical hardware-control guarantees. The uniform work-domain and residual conditions require separate certification for any concrete system, and the experimental section remains to be completed from independently verified results.
